The U.S. Department of Justice was previously ordered to respond to Apple’s document requests directed at 14 federal agencies, but the DOJ successfully obtained a temporary stay of that order while it appeals the ongoing antitrust case against Apple. Details below.

A little background

A few weeks ago, Special Master Judge Jose Linares, in the DOJ’s antitrust case against Apple, ruled in Apple’s favor and backed its document requests to 14 federal agencies.

In short, Apple wants the documents to examine how those agencies weighed privacy and security considerations when crafting smartphone policy and making procurement decisions.

Apple argues the records will help support its position that certain practices the DOJ has challenged are legitimate product differentiation and security measures — not anticompetitive restraints.

Specifically, Apple is seeking documents from the following agencies:

  • Central Intelligence Agency (CIA)
  • Department of Commerce
  • Department of Homeland Security
  • Department of Defense
  • Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI)
  • Federal Trade Commission (FTC)
  • General Services Administration
  • Department of Labor
  • National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA)
  • National Security Agency (NSA)
  • Office of the Director of National Intelligence
  • Office of Management and Budget
  • Office of Personnel Management
  • Department of State

After Judge Linares ruled in Apple’s favor, the DOJ asked him to reconsider. When Linares declined, the DOJ took the case to U.S. District Judge Julien Neals, while simultaneously asking Linares to pause the document-production order during the appeal.

Bringing us to today.

DOJ gets a temporary reprieve

Judge Linares issued an order earlier today granting the DOJ’s request to pause the document-production order so that U.S. District Judge Neals can weigh in on the government’s appeal — which is over whether the DOJ must respond to Apple’s document requests.

Judge Linares said he agreed with Apple that the DOJ “faces an uphill battle” in winning the appeal, but that on its own wasn’t enough to reject the government’s request for a stay.

He also agreed with the DOJ that it would be “manifestly unfair” to later force the 14 agencies to handle the “purportedly massive workload” of responding to Apple’s document requests if Judge Neals ultimately overturns his ruling.

Judge Linares also pushed back on Apple’s argument that pausing execution while Judge Neals weighs overturning the original ruling would hurt the company by further delaying its efforts to obtain the documents. The judge pointed out that the case remains at a “relatively early stage” of discovery, with other document collection still able to proceed in the meantime.

Now that the order is on hold, Apple will have an opportunity to respond to the government’s appeal, after which the DOJ will have seven calendar days to file its reply. Judge Neals will then decide whether to uphold or overturn Judge Linares’s original document-production order.
